content: The term Big Tobacco is a derogatory label commonly used to describe the tobacco industry as a whole, or more specifically, the three major tobacco corporations in the United States. These corporations are Philip Morris (now Altria), R.J. Reynolds (RJR), and British American Tobacco. The term may also extend to other companies with significant involvement in tobacco production and consumption, such as Lorillard or Brown & Williamson. The phrase Big Tobacco has been popularized in part by anti-smoking advocacy groups, such as the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids, and through public health campaigns funded by the Master Settlement Agreement. These efforts aim to highlight the role of the tobacco industry in promoting smoking and its associated health risks. In popular culture, Big Tobacco has been used as a symbol of corporate villainy. For example, in the comic movie Mystery Men, one of the antagonists, a cigar-smoking leader of a business-themed gang, adopts the pseudonym Big Tobacco. Additionally, the term is prominently featured in the film Thank You for Smoking, where the character Nick Naylor, played by Aaron Eckhart, serves as a lobbyist for the tobacco industry. In the movie, the character remarks on the extensive financial resources invested by the tobacco industry to make quitting smoking exceedingly difficult, emphasizing the deliberate and calculated nature of their strategies.
